article_title: Supporting Science Learning and Literacy Development Together: Initial Results from a Curriculum Study in 1st Grade Classrooms
citation: Harris, C. J., Murphy, R., Feng, M., & Rutstein, D. (2023). Supporting science learning and literacy development together: Initial results from a curriculum study in 1st grade classrooms. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Amplify Science 1st grade curriculum: three phenomena-based units integrating science and literacy
description: The Amplify Science 1st grade curriculum consists of "three phenomena-based instructional units" covering life science, physical science, and Earth and space science, each 22 lessons of 45 minutes taught over 6–8 weeks. Lessons engage students in doing, reading, writing, talking, and visualizing science, with hands-on investigations, model building, and explanation writing. The package includes a digital teacher's guide, science kit materials with literacy supports, student notebooks, and books for read-aloud, shared, and partner reading.
requirements: Teachers received 3 full days of professional learning on the curriculum's instructional stance, unit features, and lesson implementation, facilitated by the developers
constraints: Using the materials requires teachers to spend more instructional time on science than is typical based on national surveys of K–5 elementary teachers
target_learners: 1st grade students in culturally and linguistically diverse elementary school settings
target_learning_goals: Three-dimensional NGSS learning (disciplinary core ideas, science and engineering practices, crosscutting concepts)
science vocabulary in-use
reading development integrated with science
examples: In the study, intervention teachers implemented the three units within their district's NGSS-aligned science sequence while comparison teachers taught science as they typically would.
key_sources: Harris, C. J., Murphy, R., Feng, M., & Rutstein, D. (2023). Supporting science learning and literacy development together: Initial results from a curriculum study in 1st grade classrooms. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED638494

article_title: Accelerate Success for English Learners with Formative Assessment: Introduction
citation: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., & Blitz, J. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED531981
title: Ambitious teaching and learning for English learners grounded in sociocultural theory
description: The brief presents "ambitious teaching and learning" as an umbrella concept "grounded in a sociocultural theory", requiring educators to understand students' lived experiences and design learning opportunities for students to co-construct knowledge alongside peers. For English learners it means seeing them as students with promise and value rather than defined by needs and risks. It frames the seven features of high-quality EL instruction.
requirements: Educators must deeply understand who their students are and how their lived experiences and knowledge can contribute to learning
target_learning_goals: Simultaneous development of English proficiency, academic content, and analytic practices
key_sources: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., & Blitz, J. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673605

article_title: Design Principles and Observable Indicators for AI-Enabled Pedagogical Accompaniment: Evidence from the Amico Dual-Mode Prototype in Italy and China
citation: Pier Paolo Benedetti. (2026). Design Principles and Observable Indicators for AI-Enabled Pedagogical Accompaniment: Evidence from the Amico Dual-Mode Prototype in Italy and China. Accepted at the 2026 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Education (ICAIE 2026), IEEE.
title: Amico dual-mode prototype (AmicoMio and AmicoTuo) with age-sensitive configuration
description: Amico is an AI-mediated interaction device, developed as a digital agent and where feasible as a social robot, for non-clinical educational contexts, particularly technical and vocational education. AmicoMio emphasizes "precision, step-by-step reasoning, explicit framing of tasks, and concrete suggestions for action," while AmicoTuo prioritizes "maieutic questioning, reformulation, and meaning -making" without a therapeutic stance. The prototype enforces transparency of system identity, bounded sessions, dependency-prevention prompts, and data minimization, and was configured by age band (6–18, 20–40, 40–65 years) via mode-specific instruction sets and fine-tuning of the supportive mode, with per-mode sampling parameters (temperature and top-p) tuned as part of the design surface.
requirements: Operates under non-negotiable constraints: human-in-command governance, transparency of identity and limits, prevention of dependency dynamics, data minimization, and explicit orientation toward teachers, peers, and communities of practice.
constraints: Scope is intentionally limited: it does not provide curricular instruction, psychological counseling, or affective companionship, and does not optimize for content mastery through personalization; success criteria prioritize relational and governance outcomes over learning gains.
target_learners: Technical and vocational education learners across age bands 6–18, 20–40, and 40–65 years, plus adult educational actors such as teachers and parents
target_learning_goals: Task clarification, procedural orientation, reflective meaning-making, and preparation for interaction with teachers or peers
examples: Pilot participants in Italy and China engaged with both modes in structured scenarios covering task clarification, decision-making, reflection on next steps, and preparation for interaction with teachers or peers.
key_sources: Pier Paolo Benedetti. (2026). Design Principles and Observable Indicators for AI-Enabled Pedagogical Accompaniment: Evidence from the Amico Dual-Mode Prototype in Italy and China. Accepted at the 2026 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Education (ICAIE 2026), IEEE. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20665

article_title: Using Generative AI to Foster Student Sense of Belonging in Mathematics
citation: Norberg, K., Murphy, A., De Ley, L., Moltz, E.S., Almoubayyed, H., Ritter, S. (2025). Using Generative AI to Foster Student Sense of Belonging in Mathematics. In: Artificial Intelligence in Education, AIED 2025, Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol 15882. Springer, Cham. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-98465-5_24
title: AMPT: an AI tool that lets students co-author culturally relevant math word problems
description: The A.I. Math Personalization Tool (AMPT) is a generative-AI system built "to enhance cultural relevance in math word problems by giving students agency over the content." It "leverages generative AI to directly engage students as co-authors of math word problems": through scaffolded conversations students provide the context for a problem, and the AI integrates that context with the pedagogical standards of a target learning domain. Co-authored problems have been delivered to students using MATHia for additional testing.
requirements: Requires generative AI conducting scaffolded conversations that integrate student-provided context with the pedagogical standards of a target learning domain
target_learners: mathematics students using the MATHia intelligent tutoring system
target_learning_goals: mathematics word-problem learning with culturally relevant, student-chosen contexts
examples: Student-AMPT co-authored problems have been delivered to over 10,000 MATHia students for additional testing of preferences and performance
key_sources: Norberg, K., Murphy, A., De Ley, L., Moltz, E.S., Almoubayyed, H., Ritter, S. (2025). Using Generative AI to Foster Student Sense of Belonging in Mathematics. In: Artificial Intelligence in Education, AIED 2025, Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol 15882. Springer, Cham. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-98465-5_24

article_title: Knowledge elaboration: A cognitive load perspective
citation: Ramírez Ruiz, J. J. (2018). Efecto de un andamiaje de autoeficacia en el estilo cognitivo, el logro de aprendizaje y la carga cognitiva. Tesis de maestría, Universidad Pedagógica Nacional, Bogotá. https://bibliotecadigital.upn.edu.co
title: Ambiente computacional "sólidos geométricos" con andamiaje de autoeficacia (metas, autoevaluación y mensajes motivacionales)
description: Ambiente de aprendizaje computacional para geometría en educación básica primaria, compuesto por tres módulos de aprendizaje con información textual y gráfica, actividades y evaluación final de diez preguntas. La versión con andamiaje incluye una estrategia para "promover las experiencias de éxito" y hacer consciente al estudiante de sus capacidades: "El andamiaje permitió a los estudiantes elegir metas, autoevaluarse y encontrar mensajes motivacionales". La versión sin andamiaje conserva la misma estructura conceptual, interfaz, actividades y evaluación, pero carece de la estrategia motivacional.
requirements: Dos versiones comparables del ambiente (con y sin andamiaje) que compartan estructura conceptual, diseño de interfaz, actividades y evaluación final

Instrumentos de medición previos y posteriores: EFT para estilo cognitivo, subescala de autoeficacia del MSLQ, cuestionario de carga cognitiva de Leppink et al. (2014) por módulo y prueba de conocimientos final
constraints: Aplicado a estudiantes de grado quinto de una institución pública de Bogotá durante un mes y medio de interacción individual
target_learners: Estudiantes de educación básica primaria (grado quinto, edad promedio 11.30 años)
target_learning_goals: Aprendizaje de contenidos matemáticos de geometría
Percepción de autoeficacia académica
examples: Dos grupos de 47 estudiantes de quinto interactuaron con el ambiente durante mes y medio; el grupo con andamiaje se proponía metas, estrategias de navegación, autoevaluaciones y recibía mensajes motivacionales
key_sources: Ramírez Ruiz, J. J. (2018). Efecto de un andamiaje de autoeficacia en el estilo cognitivo, el logro de aprendizaje y la carga cognitiva. Tesis de maestría, Universidad Pedagógica Nacional, Bogotá. https://bibliotecadigital.upn.edu.co

article_title: The Other Side of the Coin – A Call to Investigate the Influence of Reduced Levels of Physical Activity on Children’s Cognition
citation: Herold, F., Ludyga, S., Mavilidi, M. F., Benzing, V., Vazou, S., Tomporowski, P. D., & Pesce, C. (2025). The Other Side of the Coin – A Call to Investigate the Influence of Reduced Levels of Physical Activity on Children's Cognition. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10031-5
title: Ambulatory assessment with intensive longitudinal data for physical activity-cognition research
description: Ambulatory assessment is a measurement approach in which intensive longitudinal data are captured in real-life settings with repeated within-subject assessments of physical activity (e.g., via accelerometry) and cognitive performance (e.g., via a smartphone app) at high measurement density, such as sub-daily or daily. The article proposes it to complement between-subjects analyses with within-subject analyses of "the differences between days with less or more physical activity", and recommends continuous monitoring of activity level and context across intervals of at least 7 days before, during, and after the summer break.
requirements: Repeated assessments of both the independent variable (physical activity level) and dependent variable (cognitive performance) at high measurement density
constraints: The article notes the approach's frequent within-subject active assessments for gathering contextual information can be demanding for participating children and caregivers
target_learning_goals: capturing real-life dynamic relationships between daily physical activity and cognitive performance
examples: The article describes device-initiated prompts triggered after a child spends a specific amount of time being sedentary to query the child or caregiver about the type of sedentary behavior
key_sources: Herold, F., Ludyga, S., Mavilidi, M. F., Benzing, V., Vazou, S., Tomporowski, P. D., & Pesce, C. (2025). The Other Side of the Coin – A Call to Investigate the Influence of Reduced Levels of Physical Activity on Children's Cognition. article_title: When scientific paradigms lead to tunnel vision: lessons from the study of fear
citation: Paré, D. & Quirk, G. J. (2017). When scientific paradigms lead to tunnel vision: lessons from the study of fear. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0007-4
title: Behavioral engagement model: the amygdala opposes engagement with stimuli or situations rather than coding threat
description: The article proposes replacing the threat-coding account of amygdala function with the claim that "BL activity does not promote motor inhibition per se but regulates something more general, which we refer to as behavioral engagement" — whether mammals engage with or disengage from stimuli or situations. The amygdala provides a continuous engagement-regulating signal and lets prior experience enter the decision, through plasticity affecting reinforcer value and memory consolidation. It is one of many nodes weighting motivational, contextual and mnemonic factors.
requirements: Naturalistic paradigms allowing a larger repertoire of spontaneous and learned behaviors, since paradigms restricting behavior range cannot reveal what amygdala neurons code
constraints: The term behavioral inhibition was rejected because disengaging sometimes requires motor output; whether the engagement process is deliberative in all species and conditions is unclear, per the article
target_learners: mammals in ethologically significant situations (foraging, conspecific interactions, predator confrontation)
target_learning_goals: deciding whether to engage with or disengage from stimuli and situations
examples: The model reinterprets Choi and Kim's post-inactivation risk taking as reproducing the Type-1 firing suppression required to initiate foraging, and macaque lesion effects as loss of engagement regulation
key_sources: Paré, D. & Quirk, G. J. (2017). When scientific paradigms lead to tunnel vision: lessons from the study of fear. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0007-4

article_title: When scientific paradigms lead to tunnel vision: lessons from the study of fear
citation: Paré, D. & Quirk, G. J. (2017). When scientific paradigms lead to tunnel vision: lessons from the study of fear. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0007-4
title: Sensory-to-behavioral-response transformation: a response-selection network between lateral amygdala and downstream nuclei
description: The article argues that between LA and its targets there is "a shift in the nature of the representation, from a sensory code to a behavioral response code". In downstream nuclei (BL, CeA) CS-elicited firing parallels the time course of conditioned responses, unlike the transient LA responses. A network of interconnected structures — BL, basomedial nucleus, mPFC and hippocampal formation — selects an appropriate response from alternatives (freezing, fleeing, attack, approach, reward-seeking), executed via descending projections to CeA, striatum, VMH or BNST. The authors state models based solely on potentiated LA sensory responses cannot account for behavioral flexibility when threatened.
requirements: Behavioral paradigms allowing trial-to-trial variation in the subject's decisions under fixed CS–US contingency to reveal the behavior-dependent coding
constraints: Models of fear learning solely based on potentiated sensory responses of LA neurons cannot account for behavioral flexibility such as freezing, fleeing, or attack depending on threat proximity, per the article
target_learners: mammals (rats, cats, monkeys) in aversive and appetitive conditioning
target_learning_goals: selection of appropriate defensive or appetitive responses to conditioned stimuli
examples: Figure 3 contrasts the fear-conditioning schema (LA potentiation driving freezing via CeA) with a broader network in which arbitrary CS–US pairings feed a response-selection network
key_sources: Paré, D. & Quirk, G. J. (2017). When scientific paradigms lead to tunnel vision: lessons from the study of fear. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0007-4

article_title: Leading the AI transformation in schools: it starts with a digital mindset
citation: Marcus Pietsch · Dana-Kristin Mah. (2025). Leading the AI transformation in schools: it starts with a digital mindset. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10439-w
title: Ambidextrous leadership: simultaneous opening and closing behaviors for leading innovation under paradox
description: Ambidextrous leadership holds that organizational transformation requires two leadership behaviors simultaneously: opening behavior that unleashes creativity and experimentation, and closing behavior that reduces variance and secures implementation. The article applies it to schools, mapping transformational leadership onto opening and digital instructional leadership onto closing behavior, and tests their interaction as a predictor of AI integration. As Rosing and Zacher describe it, "Opening leader behavior comprises, for example, to encourage followers to experiment with new ideas, to give room for independent thinking and acting, and to allow for learning from errors."
requirements: Leaders must demonstrate a high level of both opening and closing behaviors, operationalized methodically as an interaction of the two
constraints: The article notes a paucity of studies empirically investigating such integrative leadership approaches in schools
target_learning_goals: leading digital and AI transformation
fostering innovation in schools
examples: In the school context, a leader gives teachers freedom to experiment with digital tools (opening) while monitoring whether tool use improves instruction and achievement (closing).
key_sources: Marcus Pietsch · Dana-Kristin Mah. (2025). Leading the AI transformation in schools: it starts with a digital mindset. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10439-w

article_title: A critical evaluation of systematic reviews assessing the effect of chronic physical activity on academic achievement, cognition and the brain in children and adolescents: a systematic review.
citation: Wassenaar Thomas M., Williamson Wilby, Johansen-Berg Heidi, Dawes Helen, Roberts Nia, Foster Charlie, Sexton Claire E. (2020). A critical evaluation of systematic reviews assessing the effect of chronic physical activity on academic achievement, cognition and the brain in children and adolescents: a systematic review. The International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12966-020-00959-y
title: AMSTAR-2 critical-domain framework for rating the confidence of systematic reviews
description: AMSTAR-2 is the quality-assessment framework the article uses to rate systematic reviews by overall confidence. Confidence is determined by evaluating seven critical domains — preregistration, literature search, justification for excluding studies, risk of bias assessment, appropriateness of meta-analytical methods, risk of bias in synthesis of results, and publication bias. A lack of addressing one or multiple critical domains yields a low or critically low rating; with no critical flaws, non-critical weaknesses determine a high or moderate rating. The article applied it with two independent reviewers to all 19 reviews.
requirements: Two independent reviewers scoring the reviews
Evaluation of both critical and non-critical domains to derive an overall confidence rating
constraints: The article notes it is not recommended to combine individual item ratings into an overall score; the total score was provided only to acknowledge a quality gradient and was not used in the synthesis
target_learning_goals: evaluating evidence quality on physical activity effects on cognition, academic achievement and the brain
examples: The article rated 17 of 19 included reviews as critically low confidence because they did not address multiple critical domains
key_sources: Wassenaar Thomas M., Williamson Wilby, Johansen-Berg Heidi, Dawes Helen, Roberts Nia, Foster Charlie, Sexton Claire E. (2020). A critical evaluation of systematic reviews assessing the effect of chronic physical activity on academic achievement, cognition and the brain in children and adolescents: a systematic review. The International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12966-020-00959-y

article_title: On the Comparative Impact of Self-Assessment and Teacher-Assessment on Iranian EFL Learners' Academic Motivation
citation: Asghar Salimi, Vahid Nowrozi Larsari. (2015). On the Comparative Impact of Self-assessment and Teacher-assessment on Iranian EFL Learners' Academic Motivation. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 6(6). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.6p.74
title: Gardner's Attitude/Motivation Test Battery (AMTB) questionnaire as the motivation measure
description: The study's motivation instrument, prepared by Gardner (2004), used as both pre-test and post-test. It "includes 25 items and in front of each item six alternatives" from Strongly disagree to Strongly agree, scored on a one-to-six Likert scale. Reliability was checked with Cronbach's Alpha, and the article reports "Cronbach's Alpha Coefficient for this measurement is 0.76", above its stated 0.7 threshold. Participants answered by underlining or circling alternatives as quickly as possible.
requirements: Reliability via Cronbach's Alpha greater than 0.7, which the article reports was met at 0.76
target_learning_goals: measuring academic motivation in language learning
examples: Administered before reading-strategy teaching and again after the five-session treatment in both groups
key_sources: Asghar Salimi, Vahid Nowrozi Larsari. (2015). On the Comparative Impact of Self-assessment and Teacher-assessment on Iranian EFL Learners' Academic Motivation. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 6(6). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.6p.74

article_title: The impact of creative thinking on organizational maturity and the mediating role of experiential learning among knowledge management professionals.
citation: Nasabi Narjes Alsadat, Yusefi Ali Reza, Bordbar Najmeh. (2026). The impact of creative thinking on organizational maturity and the mediating role of experiential learning among knowledge management professionals. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-39905-6
title: Integrated Amabile–Kolb micro-to-macro model linking creative thinking, experiential learning, and organizational maturity
description: The article grounds its conceptual model in Amabile's Componential Theory of Creativity and Kolb's Experiential Learning Theory, integrated into a single framework. Creative thinking is conceptualized as "a cognitive foundation that initiates innovative thought," while experiential learning "acts as the mechanism through which these ideas are internalized and translated into practice." Kolb's theory identifies four stages — concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, and active experimentation — that support individual and organizational learning. The authors argue this combination provides a clearer micro-to-macro mechanism linking creativity, learning cycles, and organizational development than alternative models such as absorptive capacity theory, double-loop learning theory, or organizational growth lifecycle models, which emphasize systemic routines or organizational redesign.
requirements: Requires treating creative thinking, experiential learning, and organizational maturity as distinct measurable constructs within a theoretically coherent model
constraints: The authors note alternative theoretical models offer different explanations regarding how organizations convert individual creativity into structural maturity
target_learners: managers and coordinators in knowledge-intensive organizations
target_learning_goals: translating creative ideas into practical organizational practices
fostering organizational learning and development
examples: The study tested the integrated model with SEM among 505 knowledge management professionals at an Iranian medical university, finding support for partial mediation.
key_sources: Nasabi Narjes Alsadat, Yusefi Ali Reza, Bordbar Najmeh. (2026). The impact of creative thinking on organizational maturity and the mediating role of experiential learning among knowledge management professionals. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-39905-6

article_title: A cross-sectional study exploring academic motivation among rehabilitation science students under different teaching approaches in China.
citation: Hu Huiling; Luo Hongmei. (2026). A cross-sectional study exploring academic motivation among rehabilitation science students under different teaching approaches in China. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-33548-9
title: Chinese version of the Academic Motivation Scale–College (AMS-C) with seven subscales and Self-Determination Index
description: The study's measurement instrument is the Chinese AMS-C, adapted with permission from Dr. Li's research team, an SDT-based measure the article calls "one of the most widely used academic motivation measures worldwide". It has "28 questions rated on a seven-point Likert scale" equally divided into seven subscales (three intrinsic, three extrinsic, and amotivation), each scored as the mean of four items, and a Self-Determination Index formula ranging from −18 to +18.
requirements: Permissioned use of the validated Chinese adaptation; the article notes no validation studies have been conducted explicitly among Chinese rehabilitation students
constraints: Higher SDI scores are interpreted as more favorable academic performance and consequences, per the scale's source literature
target_learners: college and university students in Chinese-language higher education
target_learning_goals: measuring intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and amotivation
examples: The online questionnaire combined sociodemographic items (gender, BMI, sleep habits, teaching program) with the 28-item AMS-C
key_sources: Hu Huiling; Luo Hongmei. (2026). A cross-sectional study exploring academic motivation among rehabilitation science students under different teaching approaches in China. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-33548-9

article_title: Comparing Patient Simulation With a Humanoid Robot or a Human Actor in Terms of Training Success and Acceptance: Pilot Questionnaire Study.
citation: Schwarz P, Hellmers S, Spanknebel S, Immel D, Hurlemann R, Hein A. (2025). Comparing Patient Simulation With a Humanoid Robot or a Human Actor in Terms of Training Success and Acceptance: Pilot Questionnaire Study. JMIR Formative Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/70363
title: Humanoid robot patient (Ameca) simulation scenario for psychiatric psychopathological assessment training
description: An element consisting of the Ameca humanoid robot (Engineered Arts) programmed to present a schizophrenia patient case through "facial expressions, gestures, and speech". Videos of actor patients (12 videos of symptom combinations) served as the reproducible basis; moods, thoughts, feelings as audio tracks and matching movements were transferred via a graphical user interface to a robot management system storing symptoms that "could be presented in various combinations". The robot was evaluated as a patient simulator for training psychopathological assessment in medical and nursing education.
requirements: Videos of actor patients presenting the target symptoms as input material for programming the sequences
Expert (psychiatrist) selection of symptoms and a robot management system with a graphical user interface
constraints: The robot remains limited to preprogrammed responses and lacks spontaneity
Limited expressiveness due to the limitation of its facial muscles (number of motors in the face)
target_learning_goals: recognizing psychopathological symptoms
conducting a psychopathological assessment and making a diagnosis
examples: In the pilot, the robot presented 5 symptom sequences (flight of ideas, withdrawal of thoughts, delusions, delusional mood, thought insertion) of 0.3 to 2 minutes each
key_sources: Schwarz P, Hellmers S, Spanknebel S, Immel D, Hurlemann R, Hein A. (2025). Comparing Patient Simulation With a Humanoid Robot or a Human Actor in Terms of Training Success and Acceptance: Pilot Questionnaire Study. JMIR Formative Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/70363

article_title: Pre- and in-service teachers attribution beliefs for students' success and struggle in mathematics: first insights.
citation: Ocal Tugba, Yavuz Selim, Ocal Mehmet Fatih. (2025). Pre- and in-service teachers attribution beliefs for students’ success and struggle in mathematics: first insights. BMC Psychology 13, 703. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-025-03038-8
title: Attributions of Mathematical Excellence (AME) framework: four belief domains for explaining students' mathematics success and struggle
description: The AME framework, developed by Jacobson et al. and used as this study's primary analytic lens, extends Attribution Theory by organizing teachers' explanations of mathematical success and struggle into four belief domains. The article states it "organizes attribution types into four belief domains relevant to mathematics education: genetic (AME-G), social (AME-S), personal (AME-P), and educational (AME-E) attributions." Genetic attributions concern innate ability, social attributions concern family and environmental context, personal attributions concern effort and individual characteristics, and educational attributions concern teaching quality and resources.
requirements: Interview or survey instruments must be aligned with the four attribution domains, as this study did when constructing its interview questions
constraints: The article notes the framework may not address cross-cutting factors such as socio-economic status, and empirical subscale distinctiveness has been sparingly examined
target_learners: elementary and middle school students in mathematics
target_learning_goals: understanding and improving students' mathematics success and struggle through teachers' attributional beliefs
examples: The study coded 28 teachers' interview responses under the four AME themes using MAXQDA, with intercoder agreement of Cohen's Kappa 0.93
key_sources: Ocal Tugba, Yavuz Selim, Ocal Mehmet Fatih. (2025). Pre- and in-service teachers attribution beliefs for students’ success and struggle in mathematics: first insights. BMC Psychology 13, 703. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-025-03038-8

article_title: Artificial Intelligence-Guided Bronchoscopy is Superior to Human Expert Instruction for the Performance of Critical-Care Physicians: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Agbontaen Kaladerhan O., Cold Kristoffer M., Woods David, Grover Vimal, Aboumarie Hatem Soliman, Kaul Sundeep, Konge Lars, Singh Suveer. (2025). Artificial Intelligence-Guided Bronchoscopy is Superior to Human Expert Instruction for the Performance of Critical-Care Physicians: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Critical Care Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/CCM.0000000000006629
title: Ambu Broncho Simulator: an augmented-reality AI bronchoscopy training and feedback system
description: The Ambu Broncho Simulator is an AI navigational system using augmented reality that attaches to a bronchoscopy setup to capture procedure data and provide self-directed training. It overlays three real-time feedback features: on-screen anatomical labels that "turn from white to green" once a segment is entered, a lung tree diagram showing the bronchoscope's position, and a structured progress score awarding points for segments visited in ascending sequential order. Users can select how many feedback features are active, and the system provides automated end-of-run feedback on procedure time, diagnostic completeness, and structured progress.
requirements: Requires attachment to a bronchoscopy setup with a flexible bronchoscope, monitor, and display to capture procedure data and overlay feedback
constraints: The AI system does not provide feedback on aspects of dexterity, such as wall collision and luminal centrality
target_learning_goals: flexible bronchoscopy navigation and performance efficiency
examples: In the trial, AIG participants undertook 30 minutes of self-directed training with the system's three feedback features, with investigators on standby only for technical issues
key_sources: Agbontaen Kaladerhan O., Cold Kristoffer M., Woods David, Grover Vimal, Aboumarie Hatem Soliman, Kaul Sundeep, Konge Lars, Singh Suveer. (2025). Artificial Intelligence-Guided Bronchoscopy is Superior to Human Expert Instruction for the Performance of Critical-Care Physicians: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Critical Care Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/CCM.0000000000006629

article_title: Cochlear Implant Surgery: Virtual Reality Simulation Training and Transfer of Skills to Cadaver Dissection-A Randomized, Controlled Trial.
citation: Frendø M, Frithioff A, Konge L, Cayé-Thomasen P, Sørensen MS, Andersen SAW. (2022). Cochlear implant surgery: virtual reality simulation training and transfer of skills to cadaver dissection—A randomized, controlled trial. The Journal of International Advanced Otology. https://doi.org/10.5152/iao.2022.21429
title: Provide ample training time and mastery-learning progression when designing advanced temporal bone simulation curricula
description: For advanced otologic procedures, the article recommends curricula that give trainees enough practice to reach proficiency rather than fixed short doses. It argues that 'training revolving on attaining a set level of proficiency—that is, mastery learning—likely increases the rate of surgical skills acquisition' and that interventions should provide 'ample time for training to ensure that trainees master the procedures'.
requirements: A defined pass-fail proficiency level for progression; the article reports that a pass-fail score of 34.5 CISAT points was determined
Training volume much higher than the 2 hours given in this study to produce substantial results during cadaver dissection
constraints: Learning-curve data show that while initial training yields a substantial improvement per procedure, further training leads to progressively less learning per procedure
target_learners: Otolaryngology residents training in temporal bone surgery
target_learning_goals: Cochlear implant surgical skills
Temporal bone surgical competence
examples: In the trial, intervention trainees reached a mean of 30.4 CISAT points in the simulator, below the 34.5-point pass-fail level, after a 2-hour training dose set by course feasibility
key_sources: Frendø M, Frithioff A, Konge L, Cayé-Thomasen P, Sørensen MS, Andersen SAW. (2022). Cochlear implant surgery: virtual reality simulation training and transfer of skills to cadaver dissection—A randomized, controlled trial. The Journal of International Advanced Otology. https://doi.org/10.5152/iao.2022.21429

citation: Starosolski Michał, Kapłan Cezary, Kalemba Alicja, Majewska Karolina. (2023). title: Airway Management Outcome Score (AMOS)
description: The AMOS is a 3-point composite performance measure created by the study authors to evaluate student airway management performance in simulation, based on actions taken, their effectiveness, and their impact on the patient. AMOS=0 denotes significant or multiple errors such as "persistent, repeated attempts at a single lifeline without optimization"; AMOS=1 denotes partially successful actions; AMOS=2 denotes effective interventions with significant patient benefit. Disagreements were settled by a third blinded author.
requirements: Scoring criteria applied per Table 1, with a third blinded author carrying out independent assessment in cases of disagreement
target_learners: Medical students performing simulated airway management
target_learning_goals: Evaluating performance in simulated difficult-airway management
examples: In the study, 26/96 participants were rated AMOS=0, 30/96 as AMOS=1, and 40 as AMOS=2
